# Amazon Aurora: say it

<!-- speak:start id=aurora-s02 -->
### Prompt 1

**A customer asks.** Aurora Serverless v2 or a provisioned instance: which one should our new SaaS database use?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Both run the same Aurora. Use Serverless v2 when the load is new and uneven. Move to provisioned instances when it is steady.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both run the same Aurora engine and storage. The difference is how you size compute.

It works like this. With Serverless v2, you set a minimum and a maximum capacity.

Aurora scales each instance inside that range, even with connections open.

Capacity is counted in ACUs. One ACU is about two gibibytes of memory, with matching CPU.

A provisioned instance has a fixed instance class, with set memory and CPU.

AWS suggests serverless for spiky load, and provisioned for steady load.

The thing to watch is the minimum you set. It decides what you pay when it's quiet.

One cluster can mix both kinds, so you can change later.

In your case, I'd start with Serverless v2. When load is steady, use provisioned instances with Reserved Instances or a Database Savings Plan.

Do you know your peak yet, and how often does it come?

**Skeleton.** same engine, different sizing / a range of ACUs / minimum decides quiet cost / mix both in one cluster

**Must say.**

- With Aurora Serverless v2 you specify a minimum and maximum capacity, and Aurora scales each writer or reader inside that range.
- Scaling can happen while connections are open, because Aurora serverless does not wait for a quiet point.
- AWS says serverless is intended for variable or spiky workloads, and provisioned clusters are suitable for steady workloads.
- One Aurora cluster can hold any combination of provisioned and serverless instances.

**Do not say.**

- "Serverless is always cheaper.". Say: AWS says serverless is intended for variable or spiky workloads. Provisioned clusters are suitable for steady workloads.
- "Serverless means there is no DB instance.". Say: Aurora Serverless v2 still runs DB instances. Aurora scales each serverless writer or reader inside the capacity range you set.
- "To change later, you must build a new cluster.". Say: You can add serverless instances to an existing cluster, in any combination with provisioned instances.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Can it go down to nothing at night? Yes, if you set the minimum capacity to zero ACUs. Then the instance can pause, and you aren't charged for instance capacity while it is paused. Storage is still charged. Resuming takes approximately 15 seconds. With a minimum above zero, it doesn't pause.
- Can we move from serverless to provisioned later? Yes. One cluster can hold any combination of provisioned and serverless instances. You add the new instances to the same cluster, and Aurora doesn't make a new copy of the data.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

### Prompt 2

**A customer asks.** Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB global tables: which one gives us a second Region?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Both copy data to another Region. In Aurora, only one Region writes. In DynamoDB global tables, every Region reads and writes.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both keep a copy of your data in another Region. The difference is who can write.

It works like this. Aurora Global Database has one primary Region that takes the writes.

The secondary Regions serve reads. The lag is typically under one second.

After a Region outage, you fail over to a secondary Region.

With DynamoDB global tables, every replica reads and writes.

If one Region fails, no database failover is needed.

The thing to watch is this. An Aurora failover can lose the last writes that were not replicated.

And DynamoDB is modeled without joins, so your schema needs a new design.

In your case, the data is relational, so I'd start with Aurora Global Database.

Do your users in the second Region need to write, or mostly read?

**Skeleton.** who can write / Aurora: one writer Region / DynamoDB: every Region writes / failover loss, no joins

**Must say.**

- In an Aurora global database, only the primary cluster performs write operations.
- Aurora replicates to the secondary Regions with latency typically under a second.
- Any DynamoDB global table replica can serve reads and writes, so no database failover is needed when a Region is interrupted.
- An Aurora global database failover can lose writes that were not replicated to the chosen secondary before the event.

**Do not say.**

- "Every Aurora Region accepts writes.". Say: Only the primary cluster performs write operations. A secondary cluster can only forward writes to the primary, with write forwarding turned on.
- "An Aurora failover loses nothing.". Say: A failover can lose write transactions that were not yet replicated to the chosen secondary.
- "DynamoDB supports joins like PostgreSQL.". Say: Eliminating the need for joins is at the heart of NoSQL data modeling, so the schema needs a new design.

**Follow-up questions.**

- How fast can the second Region take over in Aurora? AWS says a secondary Region can be promoted to read and write in less than 1 minute. The user guide says the RTO can be in the order of minutes, so we plan for minutes.
- Can we move the primary back later without losing data? Yes, when all clusters are in a healthy state. A switchover moves the primary cluster to a secondary Region. It synchronizes the secondary clusters first, so the RPO is 0 (no data loss).

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

### Prompt 3

**A customer asks.** Ben wants to pay for I/O-Optimized on our main database. Is it worth it?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** It depends on one share of the bill. If I/O charges are a quarter or more of database spending, I/O-Optimized is the better choice.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: it depends on one number on our bill.

It works like this. I/O means each time the database reads or writes data on storage.

On Aurora Standard, we pay for usage and storage, plus a rate per million requests.

On I/O-Optimized, we pay only for usage and storage. I/O has no extra charge.

AWS calls I/O-Optimized the best choice when I/O is a quarter or more of database spending.

The thing to watch is the switch rule.

We can go back to Aurora Standard at any time.

But we can move to I/O-Optimized only once every thirty days.

So we decide from a full month of bills, not from one busy day.

In your case, I'd ask finance for last month's database bill, split by item.

Can finance pull that bill this week?

**Skeleton.** one number on the bill / Standard: pay per request / Optimized: no I/O charge / switch rule, full month

**Must say.**

- Aurora I/O-Optimized is the best choice when I/O spending is 25% or more of total Aurora database spending.
- With Aurora Standard you pay for usage and storage plus a standard rate per 1 million requests for I/O operations.
- With I/O-Optimized you pay only for the usage and storage of the cluster, with no additional charges for read and write I/O.
- You can switch from Standard to I/O-Optimized once every 30 days, and back to Standard at any time.

**Do not say.**

- "I/O-Optimized is always cheaper.". Say: Aurora Standard is the best choice when I/O spending is less than 25% of total Aurora database spending.
- "We can switch back and forth every week.". Say: You can switch from Standard to I/O-Optimized once every 30 days. Back to Standard is possible at any time.
- "I/O-Optimized removes the storage charge too.". Say: You still pay for the usage and storage of the cluster. Only the read and write I/O charges go away.

**Follow-up questions.**

- If a company has Aurora Reserved Instances, do they still apply? Yes. AWS says that I/O-Optimized works with existing Aurora Reserved Instances.
- What if we pick it and the bill goes up? We switch back to Aurora Standard, which is possible at any time. But the next move to I/O-Optimized has to wait, because that switch is allowed once every 30 days.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

### Prompt 4

**A customer asks.** It is still PostgreSQL. What do I get from Aurora that RDS did not give me?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** The same PostgreSQL on shared storage. Replicas read that storage, so they stay close behind, and failover usually takes under a minute.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: the same PostgreSQL, on a storage layer that all instances share.

It works like this. The cluster volume keeps six copies of your data across three Availability Zones.

Aurora Replicas read that same volume, so they don't copy the data themselves.

Replica lag is usually well under a hundred milliseconds.

And you can add up to fifteen of them, besides the primary.

One reader endpoint spreads the dashboard connections across them.

If the writer fails, a replica takes over, usually in under a minute.

The thing to watch is the bill.

On Aurora Standard, you also pay for each I/O request.

In your case, I'd move with an Aurora read replica and a short cutover.

Which dashboards break first when the replica falls behind?

**Skeleton.** same PostgreSQL, shared storage / replicas read the same volume / one reader endpoint, fast failover / the bill pays per I/O

**Must say.**

- Aurora Replicas connect to the same storage volume as the primary DB instance and support read operations only.
- Aurora Replica lag is usually much less than 100 milliseconds after the primary instance writes an update.
- The reader endpoint balances read-only connections across the Aurora Replicas of the cluster.
- If the writer fails, Aurora fails over to an Aurora Replica, and service is typically restored in less than 60 seconds.
- The code, tools and applications that work with PostgreSQL today can be used with Aurora.

**Do not say.**

- "Aurora Replicas copy the data, like RDS read replicas.". Say: Aurora Replicas connect to the same storage volume as the primary DB instance. They read the shared cluster volume.
- "Replica lag is zero.". Say: Replica lag is usually much less than 100 milliseconds, and it varies with the rate of database change.
- "Aurora is a different engine, so you rewrite the SQL.". Say: The code, tools and applications you use with PostgreSQL today can be used with Aurora.

**Follow-up questions.**

- What happens if we run only one instance, with no replica? Aurora creates a new primary instance, and service typically returns in less than 10 minutes. With an Aurora Replica, service is typically restored in less than 60 seconds. So for fast failover we keep a replica.
- How do we move without a long outage? We create an Aurora read replica of the RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. For the cutover, we stop all writes on the RDS instance. When the replica lag is zero, we stop replication and make it a standalone Aurora cluster. Then the application connects to the new cluster.

</details>
